newsitem.title: KUWAIT: More attacks on Iraq possible, U.S. says.
newsitem.headline: More attacks on Iraq possible, U.S. says.

text.p: U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry said on Sunday further strikes on Iraq were still a possibility and announced he wanted Kuwait to allow in 5,000 more U.S. troops to boost American might in the oil-rich Gulf.
Asked if more U.S. strikes against Iraq were still possible, Perry told a news conference on a brief visit to Kuwait: "Yes, it is still a possibility."

He added the United States "will take whatever action is necessary" to enforce an expanded southern Iraqi no-fly zone up to the 33rd parallel, which runs 50 km (30 miles) south of Baghdad, and to protect the pilots who patrol it.
Perry also said he had asked Kuwait's emir, Sheikh Jaber al-Ahmad al-Sabah, for permission to proceed with a previously announced plan to deploy 5,000 U.S. troops in the Gulf state.
The emir had replied that Kuwait would say whether it would permit the deployment of the troops after the issue had been discussed by Kuwait's Supreme Defence Council, Perry said.
Perry is on a visit to the Gulf to try to rally the Gulf War alliance against Iraqi President Saddam Hussein following Iraqi missile attacks against U.S. planes patrolling the no-fly zone.

Perry, who arrived in Kuwait on Sunday after a short visit to neighbouring Saudi Arabia, also met Kuwait's Crown Prince and Prime Minister Sheikh Saad al-Abdulla al-Sabah and Defence Minister Sheikh Ahmad Hamoud al-Jaber al-Sabah at Kuwait international airport.

Perry will also visit a number of members of the six-country Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) economic and military alliance, as well as non-Arab regional ally Turkey. The GCC groups Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Oman and Bahrain.

Earlier on Sunday in Saudi Arabia, Perry held talks with Saudi officials and also travelled to al-Kharg airbase 100 km (60 miles) southwest of the capital Riyadh to inspect security for U.S. forces stationed there.
Saudi Arabia, eager thus far not to appear as being directly involved in the current U.S. military buildup in the Gulf, has so far kept silent about Perry's visit.

Kuwait, grateful to Washington for leading the 1991 Gulf War that liberated it from a seven-month Iraqi occupation, is so far the only Arab country to support Washington in its latest standoff with Saddam.
But Kuwaiti Foreign Minister Sheikh Sabah al-Ahmad al-Jaber al-Sabah said on Sunday there was no question of U.S. land forces crossing into Iraq from Kuwait.

"There is no passage for land forces, but there are air forces at Kuwaiti bases and this is not something new and they are also present in other states in the Gulf," he told reporters in the Egyptian city of Alexandria.
Eight Stealth bombers landed in Kuwait on Friday for a possible military strike against Iraq.

The Arab League, which groups all Arabs states including Iraq and Washington's close allies in the Gulf, condemned U.S. cruise missile attacks on Iraq this month, saying they violated Iraqi sovereignty.
While most of its regional allies are unwilling to take part, Washington has pressed on with the buildup in the region, including sending a second aircraft carrier battle group.
U.S. President Bill Clinton said on Saturday he had placed a "strategic strait-jacket" on Saddam by sending enough military force to the Gulf to keep him in check.
Kuwait has not spelled out publicly the measures it would like to see Washington take against Saddam and is waiting to hear a detailed exposition of Clinton's goals, diplomats said.
